newsitem.title: INDONESIA: ASEAN leaders meet to discuss trade, Burma.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN leaders meet to discuss trade, Burma.

text.p: The heads of seven Southeast Asian nations met on Saturday for their annual summit which officials said would focus on trade issues and the question of when to admit Burma into the group.
A smiling President Suharto welcomed leaders from Brunei, the Philippines, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam at the summit venue in the ballroom of a luxury Jakarta hotel.

In keeping with the concept that it was an informal summit, all seven leaders from the Association of South East Nations (ASEAN) were dressed in long-sleeved batik shirts embossed with patterns in yellow and gold.
No aides were present and there was no fixed agenda.
Heads of government from observer nations Burma, Laos and Cambodia were to join the full members later in the day.

"The indicative list of topics we have submitted has a very long list of subjects," Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi told reporters. "The leaders can choose from ASEAN, regional and international issues."
But he said the summit would be dominated by next month's inaugural meeting in Singapore of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) -- the global trade regulatory body -- and Burma.
On the WTO meeting, Abdullah Ahmad said: "Other regional bodies have expressed their views. ASEAN has not done it at the summit level."
ASEAN nations have criticised Western moves to include labour and human rights in trade and investment issues and the summit is expected to endorse this stand, diplomats said.
The leaders would also discuss Burma, Badawi and other officials said.
Rangoon has applied for full membership in ASEAN and had hoped to be admitted along with Cambodia and Laos next year.

But the military government's crackdown on the pro-democracy movement of Nobel peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi has led to protests from Western nations and human rights activists, who have said admitting Burma into a prestigious club like ASEAN would be tantamount to approval of its domestic policies.
Burma has detained and released nearly 1,000 people in various crackdowns on the democracy movement since May.

A U.N. panel earlier this week rebuked Burma's military rulers for suppressing political opponents, using forced labour to build its economy, torturing prisoners, abusing women and conducting summary executions.
ASEAN leaders have said in the past that the membership issue is solely to be decided by the group itself.
But President Fidel Ramos of the Philippines and Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong have said in the past month that Burma might not yet be ready for full membership.
Both, however, stressed that the principle of admitting Burma was not in question, just the timing.
ASEAN Secretary-General Ajit Singh told reporters Burma was technically equipped for full membership.
"As far as technical preparations go, Myanmar (Burma) is well-prepared to join the ASEAN Free Trade Area," he said, adding that a final decision would likely be taken at the summit.
Diplomats have said Malaysia and Indonesia could back Burma's bid for early admission.
Asked if all 10 southeast Asian nations would become full members by the time ASEAN's 30th anniversary celebrations are held in Kuala Lumpur next July, Badawi said: "Hopefully."
Meanwhile, Burmese military leader General Than Shwe held discussions with Ramos before the summit started. Diplomats said the meeting went well, but refused to give details.
Another topic expected to be discussed was the setting up of rail links between Singapore and Kunming in southern China, Malaysia's Abdullah Ahmad said.
The existing link between Singapore and Bangkok would be extended north through Indochina and discussions with Laos and Cambodia would be required to come to an agreement on the project, he said.
